newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: New players, old game for control of Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: New players, old game for control of Afghanistan.

text.p: The participants are new but the "great game" played out over Afghanistan is centuries old -- how to tame the lawless country and open a path from the deserts of landlocked Central Asia south to the Arabian Sea.
Napoleon Bonaparte and Russia's Tsar Alexander I saw Afghanistan as a potential invasion path to wrest control of Britain's Indian possessions.

Neither ruler had much idea of the tracts of inhospitable desert, icy mountain passes and the wild tribes that dwelt in them. But the plan was enough to send shivers down the straight spines of British imperial policy makers.
Games of diplomatic bluff and treacherous alliances with armed factions have changed little. The melting of Soviet border in 1991 has made the path through Afghanistan as prized as ever.
This time the desired route is to export billions of dollars worth of oil and gas from the former Soviet republics of Central Asia to booming south Asian markets.
South Asian states like Pakistan see a potential market for their own goods among Central Asia's 60 million people, much as Britain's East India Company did more than a century ago.
Washington, anxious to ensure Central Asia remains out of the Kremlin's clutches but frustrated by its ice-cold relations with Iran, also sees business opportunities.
UNOCAL Corp of the United States has ambitious plans to build a $2 billion gas pipeline to transport Turkmen gas through Afghanistan to Pakistan. An oil pipeline would follow.
But any hopes of forging a path through Afghanistan, be it with steel pipes or camel trains, are reliant on that most elusive ingredient in Afghan politics -- peace.
Pakistan, a major player in today's game, sent its foreign minister last week to explain to Central Asian leaders why it has recognised Afghanistan's purist Islamic Taleban militia.
Pakistan's bet, like many before it, is that this faction looks the best means of bringing unity and stability to the fractious country.
"They control 22 of 32 provinces, they control the capital Kabul," Pakistani Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan told reporters in the Kazakh capital Almaty last week.
On the face of it, Central Asia, anxious to break its dependence on Kremlin-controlled pipelines and trade routes to the north, should be interested in Pakistan's Taleban sell.
But Central Asian reaction to Ayub Khan's visit, which included an invitation to an "intra-Afghan" peace talks in Islamabad, was unenthusiastic.

"We will support any peace efforts," said Kazakhstan's stony-faced foreign minister, Kasymzhomart Tokayev. His government as well as those of the other Central Asian states recognise the government of Burhanuddin Rabbani, ousted by the Taleban from Kabul last year.
"Neither of them looked like they wanted to meet one another," said one Western diplomat.
Underlying Central Asia's distrust of Pakistan is an old ethnic divide and a more modern worry over the existence of radical Islam on the ex-Soviet states' doorsteps.

Central Asian leaders see the Taleban as a Pakistani creation. Many of their black-turbaned number were recruited in the Afghan refugee camps of Pakistan's Northwest Frontier Province and are predominantly fiercely traditional Pashtuns.
They could hardly be more different from the forces of the Uzbek faction leader, General Abdul Rashid Dostum, based in the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif.
His officers dress in crisp olive Soviet army surplus, his men carry a razor in their packs to distinguish their clean-shaven chins from the straggle-bearded men from the south.
Uzbek troops are also partial to hard Russian vodka, a taste picked up from Soviet advisers they allied with during Moscow's disastrous invasion of Afghanistan in the 1980s.

Uzbekistan's president, Islam Karimov, has described Dostum as all that stands between the Taleban and his nation. The warlord has access to the Friendship Bridge across the Amu Darya river and over which Soviet troops withdrew in 1989.
Differences with the Taleban are just as sharp to the ethnic Tajiks under the command of ousted government commander and famed "lion of the Panjsher", Ahmad Shah Masood.
Tajikistan has made an airport available to Masood from which to ferry supplies to his fastness in the Panjsher Valley.
The Central Asian states worry a flood of refugee ethnic kin from a Taleban-controlled Afghanistan would destabilise their own states, already battered by post-communist uncertainties.

Islam is also a concern for the regions' leaders, many of them former Communist Party bosses, who were aghast when one of the first acts of the Taleban fighters when they took Kabul was to execute Afghanistan's ex-Communist leader, Najibullah.

Uzbekistan's Karimov is determined to stamp out any vestiges of radical Islam in his own republic, imprisoning radical clerics and clamping down on the wearing of the veil, according to human rights groups.

Seventy years of Soviet rule failed to destroy Islam among Uzbekistan's mostly rural 23 million population, merely driving it underground. With secular opposition in the republic largely crushed, any of thousands of new mosques could -- and have -- become a forum of discontent.
So the Taleban are an unwelcome model. Asked to comment on Ayub Khan's visit last week, one Uzbek official sighed: "There is an official taboo on discussion of the situation in Afghanistan here."
